full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. The learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong dismissed the application for pre-emption. On appeal the learned District Judge, Chittagong, set aside the Judgment of the trial Court and allowed the application for pre-emption in part. 

 3. The case of the preempted-petitioner in brief, was that, he purchased the case land in said certificate case on 24.10.73 for Tk. 9000/-. The petitioner got delivery of possession on 11.2.74 through court. After getting possession the petitioner constructed C.I. huts on the hills and another but at the bottom of the hill in March and April. 1974. The petitioner after the auction purchase paid an amount of Tk. 80,000/- to the servant Mofizullah and to the relation of H.E. Percival for the price of the structures standing on the case land. According to the petitioner he also made payment of Tk. 10,000/- to Mofizullah at the request of the son of H.E. Percival. The petitioner spent about 20,000/-. for improvement of the case land after auction purchase. The pre-emptee has denied the date of knowledge of the preempted from 3.1.76. According to the pre-emptee, the pre-emptor knew about the sale from before. According to the present petitioner, the pre-emptors are not co-sharers in P.S. khatian No 14 which was auction purchased by the petitioner for arrears of rent as the remaining land of khatian No. 14 was separated by Misc. case No. 89/72-73. According to the pre-emptee, the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer in old khatian No. 14 as the old khatian No. 14 merged into P.S. khatian No. 18 and this khatian was put to auction sale and the pre-emptor did not remain a co-sharer. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record dismissed the application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. On appeal the learned District Judge allowed the application for pre-emption in part and remanded the case to the trial court for assessment of the costs of improvement in the case. Mr. S. R. Pal, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee petitioner has submitted mainly two grounds for my consideration. Firstly, the learned Advocate or the petitioner has submitted that the learned lower appellate Court acted illegally and with material irregularity in holding in a summary jurisdiction that the amalgamation and separation of Tenancy in Misc. Case No. 89/72-73 is illegal, null and void and without jurisdiction and further committing illegality in holding that the pre-emptor continued to remain a co-sharer in Khatian No. 24. Secondly, he has contended that the application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not maintainable in view of the bar under section 85 (2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 1 will proceed to consider the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner hereinafter. 

 5. Thus, in the background of the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant findings of fact on the question of notice in the proceeding in separation and amalgamation, the relevant laws on the subject are to he carefully considered in this proceeding. Section 116 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as follows :— 

 "116—Amalgamation of holding of a Tenant in the same village. Where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject to separate tenancies, such parcels of land shall, under the orders of the Revenue Officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. 

 Section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy read as follows :— 

 (c) for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to hint by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing, such sub-division of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any as he may consider fair and equitable : 

 6. Thus, from the reading of the relevant provisions of sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is clear that a Revenue Officer is competent to start with the proceeding of amalgamation, consolidation and subdivision of a tenancy but for this purpose namely, for amalgamation and consolidation the proceeding may be started either on the own motion of the Revenue Officer or on an application made in that behalf by one or more co-sharer tenants. But clause (c) of section 117 says that for sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent an application a to be made by one or more co-sharer-tenants and on this application by the tenants concerned the Revenue Officer by order in writing direct such sub-division of a joint tenancy as he may consider fair and equitable. Thus it is clear that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application is to be made by the parties and the Revenue Officer has got no authority on his own motion to sub-division a joint tenancy. The amalgamation and consolidation as have been referred in the section may begin for the purpose of consolidation and amalgamation of holding for the purpose of collection on revenue and for that purpose the Revenue Officer may on his own motion exercise jurisdiction. This power has been given under sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy the legislature though it lit and proper that such a sub-division is only permissible on the application of one of more co-sharer tenants as the interests of the tenants are primary concerned in the scheme of sub-division of a joint tenancy. Thus, it is clear that the legislature provided that the sub-division of a holding may be made when notice has been given to the parties concerned for appearance and being heard in the matter. That it is clear that the legislature intended that when any co-sharer tenant wants division of a holding such a proceeding can be taken. So, I am of the view that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application must be filed by the tenant concerned. In the instant case the typed copy of the application dated 12.3.69 in the certificate caws before the Certificate Officer at Chittagong Under section 9 of the P.D.R. Act for dismissing the certificate cases could not be roe wale brought in the Misc. Case No. 89/72-73 by the Revenue Officer. I have held earlier that there was in fact no application by H.E. Percival for amalgamation and separation of his holding. The courts below were also of the view that this power was exercised suo-motu by the Revenue Officer in this Misc. proceeding for amalgamation and separation. I may point out here that the application of H. E. Percival denying his liability In respect of the certificate cases was dated 12.3.69 and this proceeding for amalgamation and separation started on 17.3.73 after about 4 years and the admitted position being that H. E. Percival died in August, 1971, the question of filing this application by H.E. Percival thus, in fact, does not arise. Thus, this was a suo-motu exercise of power by the concerned Revenue Officer in this behalf. A reference to the provision of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shows that no order shall be passed unless a notice is given the parties concerned and the matter is heard. This proviso clearly indicates that notice is a must to the partied concerned in cases of amalgamation, consolidation and sub-division without service of notice on the parties concerned no final order can be passed in the matter of amalgamation, consolidation and sub-division. Thus, after careful consideration of the relevant provisions of sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act I am of the opinion that no proceeding for sub-division of a joint tenancy can be taken without any application by a tenant and in that proceeding notices must be served on the parties concerned. I have indicated earlier that in the instant case there was no application for amalgamation and separation by the tenants and the Lower Appellate Court has correctly come to a finding from the perusal of the records of the Misc. proceeding No. 89/72-73 that no notices were served on the parties concerned and consequently the lower appellate court rightly held that the proceeding taken under amalgamation and separation of the holding was null and void and the same is liable to be set aside. 

 7. Thus after a careful consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant provisions of law as discussed above I had no substance in the first point raised by S.R. Pal in this behalf. Incidentally, I may point out here that proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for pre-emption is no doubt a summary proceeding but since the question of amalgamation and separation in the proceeding as mentioned above is relevant for the purpose of determination of the fact whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in khatian No. 14 or not, the courts below very rightly proceeded to see whether the tenancy has been separated in accordance with law thereby the pre-emptor remained a re-sharer or ceased to be a co-sharer. Thus the contention of Mr. S. R. Pal that in a summary proceeding in the courts below should not have gone to determine the legality or otherwise of amalgamation and separation of tenancy is without any substance. 

 8. Thus I hold that the pre-emptor continued to remain a co-sharer in the Malian No. 14 as if there was no separation under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such the pre-emptor was competent to file an application for pre-emption and the lower appellate court has correctly decided this point by holding that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer and he had locus stanch to file this application for pre-emption. 

 9. Now coming to the second point raised by Mr. S. R. Pal that an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not maintainable in view of the Bar under section 85(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, it will be seen that section 85(2) does not bar an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Section 85(2) of the Act reads as follows "nothing 'in this act shall apply to any non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Central or Provincial Government :— 

 10. In the connection a reference may be made to the case of Haji Aktaruzzaman Vs. Jadunath Pal and another reported in 17 D.L.R. 384. A Full Bench of the Dacca High Court considered section 80(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and in paragraph 16 of that reported decision as follows: 

 In the light of the proviso to section 85(3) of the Act a tenant in respect of non-agricultural land would not be deprived of a right reposed in him by the provisions of Act on the only ground of acquisition of superior tight in the land by Government. The right vested in a tenancy by the provisions of the Act in the right to take advantage of the provisions of the Act, including a right which is immediately enforceable and also a right which is enforceable in future, on the happening of a contingency. The aforesaid answer will also apply in respect of an application under section 24 of the Act. We hold that section 85(2) of the Act does not bee the application filed by the opposite parties under section 24 of the Act. We also hold that the case reported in 16 D.L.R. 77, in which it held that such an application under section 24 was competent, was correctly decided although we have come to the same conclusion by a somewhat different process of reasoning."
